'''''Strobilanthes kunthiana''''', known as '''Kurinji''' or '''Neelakurinji''' in [[Tamil language]] and [[Malayalam]] and '''Gurige''' in [[Kannada]], is a [[shrub]] of the bear's breeches family ([[Acanthaceae]]) that is found in the [[shola]] forests of the [[Western Ghats]] in [[Kerala]], [[Karnataka]] and [[Tamil Nadu]]. The purplish blue flower blossoms only once in 12 years, and gave the [[Nilgiri Mountains]] range its name as ''nil'' (blue) + ''giri'' (mountains). Of all long interval bloomers (or [[plietesials]]) ''Strobilanthes kunthiana'' is the most rigorously demonstrated, with documented bloomings in 1838, 1850, 1862, 1874, 1886, 1898, 1910, 1922, 1934,<ref>{{ cite journal | last= Robinson |first= M.E. | date= 1935 | title= The Flowering of Strobilanthes | journal= Journal of the Bombay Natural History Society | volume= 38 | pages= 117–122}}</ref> 1946, 1958, 1970,<ref>{{cite book |editor-last1= Burley |editor-last2= Styles | date= 1976 | title= Tropical Trees | location= London | publisher= Academic Press | pages= 138–139 }}</ref> 1982, 1994, 2006,<ref>Frontline periodical Volume 23 Issue 17 (26 August 2006)</ref> 2018, and 2026, these have no match to Solar cycles. This plant flowers during September–October.

==Description==
Kurinji grows at an altitude of 1300 meters to 2400 metres. The plant is usually 30 to 60 cm high. They can, however, grow well beyond 180 cm under congenial conditions.<ref name="SK">Save Kurinji Campaign,  [http://kurinji.in] Flower of the blue mountains]</ref>

The kurinji plant belongs to the [[genus]] ''[[Strobilanthes]]'' which was first scientifically described by [[Christian Gottfried Daniel Nees von Esenbeck]] in the 19th century.  The genus has around 250 species, of which at least 46 are found in India. Most of these species show an unusual flowering behaviour, varying from annual to 16-year blooming cycles.<ref name="frontline">{{cite web |url=http://www.hinduonnet.com/fline/fl2317/stories/20060908001106600.htm |title=Kurinji crown |magazine=Frontline |date=8 September 2006  |author= |access-date= 21 October 2007 |url-status=usurped |archive-date=2007-10-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071021105803/http://www.hinduonnet.com/fline/fl2317/stories/20060908001106600.htm}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.munnar.holiday/neelakurinji-flowers-munnar-bloom/ |title=Neelakurinji Flowering Season 2018-When Munnar Blooms Blue in 2018|date=2018-02-21 }}</ref>

Plants that bloom at long intervals like ''Strobilanthes kunthiana'' are known as [[plietesials]]. Other commonly used expressions or terms which apply to part or all of the plietesial life history include gregarious flowering, [[Mast (botany)#Mast seeding|mast seeding]] and supra-annual synchronized semelparity (semelparity = monocarpy).<ref>Daniel,  Thomas F.  2006.  [http://researcharchive.calacademy.org/research/scipubs/pdfs/v57/proccas_v57_n38.pdf Synchronous Flowering and Monocarpy Suggest Plietesial Life History for Neotropical ''Stenostephanus chiapensis'' (Acanthaceae).] Proceedings of the California Academy of Sciences. Fourth Series. Volume 57, No. 38, pp. 1011–1018, 1 fig. 28 December 2006</ref>

Other ''kurinji'' species, such as ''[[Strobilanthes cuspidatus]]'', bloom once every seven years, and then die. Their seeds subsequently sprout and continue the cycle of life and death.<ref>{{cite news |date=14 November 2016 |title=Wonder flower in bloom again |work=The Hindu |url=http://newsite.thehindu.com/news/cities/Coimbatore/Wonder-flower-in-bloom-again/article16381500.ece?homepage=true |access-date=14 November 2016}}</ref>
[[File:Strobilanthes kunthianus in Kurunji. ..jpg|thumb|A hillside with mass flowering in 2018]]

===Masting===
Some species of ''Strobilanthes'' are examples of a mass seeding phenomenon termed as [[masting]]<ref>Kelly, D. 1994. [http://www.biol.canterbury.ac.nz/masting/pdfs/Kelly94TREE.pdf The evolutionary ecology of mast seeding (PDF)]. Trends Ecol. Evol.. 9(12): 465-470. Accessed on 24 January 2010</ref> which can be defined as "synchronous production of seed at long intervals by a population of plants".<ref>Janzen (1976) in Annul. Rev. Ecol. Syst., 7, 347-391</ref> Strict masting only occurs in species that are [[monocarpic]] (or [[semelparous]]) -- individuals of the species only reproduce once during their lifetime, then die,<ref>[http://www.ubcbotanicalgarden.org/potd/2009/01/strobilanthes_callosus.php Strobilanthes callosus; Botany Photo of the Day] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100926114910/http://www.ubcbotanicalgarden.org/potd/2009/01/strobilanthes_callosus.php |date=2010-09-26 }}; Notes posted by Daniel Mosquin; 13 January 2009</ref> as is the case with ''Strobilanthes kunthiana''.

== Etymology ==
The plant's common name is derived from the [[Tamil language|Tamil]] words ''neelam'', meaning the colour blue, and ''kurinji'', the flower that defines the [[Kurinji (thinai)|mountainous ecoregion]] described in classical [[Sangam literature|Sangam Literature]], where it blooms in abundance. <ref>{{Cite web |last=Tourism |first=South |title=Kurinji Flower – Treasure Of Tamilnadu {{!}} South Tourism |url=https://www.southtourism.in/kurinji.php |access-date=2026-09-09 |website=www.southtourism.in |language=en}}</ref>

==Habitat==
Kurinji once used to cover the [[Anamalai Hills]], [[Cardamom Hills]], [[Nilgiri Hills]], [[Palani Hills]], [[Kudremukh]] and [[Bababudangiri]] like a carpet during its flowering season. Now plantations and dwellings occupy much of their habitat. Neelakurinji also bloomed in Chandra Drona Hill Ranges (Bababudan Giri) in [[Chikkamagaluru]] district of Karnataka in 2006. The whole of Bababudangiri Hills (Datta Peeta) were covered in a carpet of bluish purple flowers. It last bloomed in 2018.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-01-13 |title=Neelkarunji-the flowers that blossom once in 12 years |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/etimes/trending/the-season-of-neelakarunji-flowers-that-bloom-once-in-12-years-is-back/photostory/106808933.cms?picid=106808942 |access-date=2025-09-19 |work=The Times of India |issn=0971-8257}}</ref>  Besides the Western Ghats, Neelakurinji is also seen in the [[Shevroy]] in the [[Eastern Ghats]], [[Sanduru]] hills of [[Bellary]] district in Karnataka.

In 2006, Neelakurunji flowered again in [[Kerala]] and [[Tamil Nadu]] after a gap of 12 years.

In 2017, Neelakurinji flowers bloomed in the hills behind Kumaraswamy temple in [[Sanduru]], [[Bellary]] district.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://bangaloremirror.indiatimes.com/news/state/karnataka-12-year-wonder-in-full-bloom/articleshow/60467459.cms|title=Karnataka: 12-year wonder in full bloom|work=Bangalore Mirror|access-date=2018-07-13}}</ref>

==Conservation==
[[Kurinjimala Sanctuary]] protects the kurinji in approximately 32 km<sup>2</sup> core habitat in [[Kottakamboor]] and [[Vattavada]] villages in [[Idukki district]] of [[Kerala]]. The Save Kurinji Campaign Council organizes campaigns and, programs for conservation of the [[Kurinji]] plant and its habit.<ref name=SK/> Kurinji Andavar temple located in [[Kodaikanal]] on [[Tamil Nadu]] dedicated to [[Tamils|Tamil]] God [[Murugan]] also preserves Strobilanthes plants.

== Cultural significance ==
The [[Paliyan]] tribal people living in Tamil Nadu use the plant's flowering cycle as a reference to calculate their age.<ref>{{cite web |author=Mike Kielty |date=2008-03-04 |title=The Lost Gardens of the Raj |url=http://www.tcs.cam.ac.uk/impact/features/the-lost-gardens-of-the-raj |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120912102131/http://www.tcs.cam.ac.uk/impact/features/the-lost-gardens-of-the-raj/ |archive-date=2012-09-12 |publisher=The Cambridge Student Online}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-10-16 |title=India's flower that blooms every 12 years |url=https://www.bbc.com/travel/article/20181015-the-flower-that-blooms-every-12-years |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=www.bbc.com |language=en-GB}}</ref>  

==References in literature==
Kurinji flower is used to describe the associated mountainous landscape where it blooms in Sangam Literature [[Sangam literature|classical Tamil literature]]. The historical novel, ''Kurinji Flowers'' by Clare Flynn features the neelakurinji as a backdrop to a tragic love affair in 1940s India.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Flynn|first1=Clare|title=Kurinji Flowers|date=8 October 2014|publisher=Cranbrook Press|location=London}}</ref>      [[File:Kurinji.jpg|thumb|Kurinji]]
